questions.question: Several bidders compete for one object. Which description defines a common-value auction?
options: All value it at the same unknown $v$; each sees a private signal about $v$.
Each bidder knows her own value, and all bidders happen to have the same value.
The object is worth the same $v$ to all, and $v$ is announced before bidding.
Each bidder's value is her own signal, and signals are independent across bidders.

questions.question: Which of these auctions is best described as a common-value auction?
options: A painting bought to hang at home, each bidder knowing how much she likes it.
A concert ticket for one evening, each bidder knowing whether she is free that night.
Drilling rights to an oil field of unknown size, each bidder holding a survey estimate.
A meal voucher for a restaurant, each bidder knowing how hungry she will be.

questions.question: In a second-price auction (the higher bid wins and pays the other bid) with a common value $v$ and private signals, why does the private-value argument for bidding one's value break down?
options: She does not know $v$, so 'bid your value' is not a rule she can follow.
The argument breaks down because in this format the winner pays her own bid.
The argument breaks down because common values make all bids equal.
It does not break down: bidding one's own signal is weakly dominant.

questions.question: Two bidders compete for an object worth $v=\theta_1+\theta_2$ to each; bidder $i$ privately observes $\theta_i$, and $\theta_1,\theta_2$ are i.i.d. uniform on $[0,1]$. What is $\mathbb{E}[v\mid\theta_1=0.8,\ \theta_2<0.8]$, bidder 1's expected value given her signal and that the rival's signal is lower?

Two bidders compete for an object worth $v=\theta_1+\theta_2$ to each; bidder $i$ privately observes $\theta_i$, and $\theta_1,\theta_2$ are i.i.d. uniform on $[0,1]$. The higher bid wins and pays its own bid (first-price). In the symmetric equilibrium $b(\theta)=\theta$. A bidder with signal $0.7$ bids $0.7$. What is her expected margin, $\mathbb{E}[v\mid\text{she wins}]-0.7$?

Two bidders compete for an object worth $v=\theta_1+\theta_2$ to each; bidder $i$ privately observes $\theta_i$, and $\theta_1,\theta_2$ are i.i.d. uniform on $[0,1]$. The higher bid wins and pays the other bid (second-price). Both bidders use $b(\theta)=2\theta$. What is the seller's expected revenue?
In a common-value auction with private signals, bidders use a symmetric increasing bidding function. Which expected value should a bidder use when deciding what winning is worth?
options: $\mathbb{E}[v\mid\theta_i]$, since her signal is all the information she has at the time of bidding.
$\mathbb{E}[v]$, since all bidders share the same value $v$.
Her signal $\theta_i$, since it is an estimate of the common value $v$.
$\mathbb{E}[v\mid\theta_i,\ i\text{ wins}]$, since winning reveals the rivals' signals are lower.

questions.question: Two bidders compete for an object worth $v=\theta_1+\theta_2$ to each; bidder $i$ privately observes $\theta_i$, and $\theta_1,\theta_2$ are i.i.d. uniform on $[0,1]$. The symmetric equilibrium bid is $2\theta$ when the winner pays the other bid, but $\theta$ when the winner pays her own bid. Why is the second bid lower?
options: With her own bid as price, winning carries no information, so she bids her signal.
Paying her own bid, the winner gains only by bidding below her expected value.
Paying her own bid makes winning more likely, so she can afford to bid less.
Expected revenue is lower when the winner pays her own bid, so bids must be lower.

questions.question: In a common-value auction the object is worth the same unknown $v$ to every bidder, and each bidder privately observes a signal $\theta_i$ about $v$. Payments are transfers between the winner and the seller, so the total surplus of the sale is the winner's value of the object. Does it matter for this total surplus which bidder wins?
options: Yes: the bidder with the highest signal values the object most, so she should win.
Yes: the object should go to the bidder whose signal estimates $v$ most accurately.
No: every bidder values the object at the same $v$, so any winner gives surplus $v$.
No: nobody knows $v$, so the total surplus of an allocation is not defined at all.

questions.question: Two bidders compete for an object worth $v=\theta_1+\theta_2$ to each; bidder $i$ privately observes $\theta_i$, and $\theta_1,\theta_2$ are i.i.d. uniform on $[0,1]$. The higher bid wins and pays the other bid (second-price). The rival bids $2\theta_2$. A bidder with signal $0.6$ bids $1.6$ instead of $1.2$. What is her expected payoff?

Two bidders compete for an object worth $v=\theta_1+\theta_2$ to each; bidder $i$ privately observes $\theta_i$, and $\theta_1,\theta_2$ are i.i.d. uniform on $[0,1]$. The higher bid wins and pays its own bid (first-price). The rival bids $\theta_2$. A bidder with signal $0.7$ bids $0.5$ instead of $0.7$. What is her expected payoff?

Two bidders compete for an object worth $v=\theta_1+\theta_2$ to each; bidder $i$ privately observes $\theta_i$, and $\theta_1,\theta_2$ are i.i.d. uniform on $[0,1]$. The higher bid wins and pays the other bid (second-price). The rival bids $2\theta_2$. Why should a bidder with signal $x$ not shade her bid to $\mathbb{E}[v\mid\theta_1=x,\ \theta_2<x]=1.5x$?
options: Because $1.5x$ overstates the value when she wins, so she should bid even lower.
Because she should bid $\mathbb{E}[v\mid\theta_1=x]=x+0.5$, ignoring the rival.
Because shading never pays when the winner pays the rival's bid.
Bidding $2x$ adds wins with $0.75x<\theta_2<x$, each giving $x-\theta_2>0$.

questions.question: Two bidders compete for an object worth $v=\theta_1+\theta_2$ to each; bidder $i$ privately observes $\theta_i$, and $\theta_1,\theta_2$ are i.i.d. uniform on $[0,1]$. The higher bid wins and pays the other bid (second-price). In equilibrium a bidder with signal $x$ bids $2x$, which exceeds $\mathbb{E}[v\mid\theta_1=x,\ \theta_2<x]=1.5x$. Does this mean she loses money on average when she wins?
options: Yes: she pays more than the expected value of the object given that she wins.
No: she pays $2\theta_2$, which is below $x+\theta_2$ whenever she wins.
Yes, but the loss is offset by the cases in which she loses the auction.
No: she pays exactly $1.5x$, the expected value given that she wins.

questions.question: Two bidders compete for an object worth $v=\theta_1+\theta_2$ to each; bidder $i$ privately observes $\theta_i$, and $\theta_1,\theta_2$ are i.i.d. uniform on $[0,1]$. The higher bid wins and pays the other bid (second-price). The rival bids $3\theta_2$ (not the equilibrium rule). Which bid gives a bidder with signal $0.6$ the highest expected payoff?

Two bidders compete for an object worth $v=\theta_1+\theta_2+\tfrac{1}{2}$ to each; bidder $i$ privately observes $\theta_i$, i.i.d. uniform on $[0,1]$. The higher bid wins and pays the other bid (second-price). Both use the same increasing bidding function in a symmetric equilibrium. What does a bidder with signal $0.3$ bid?

With private values, the Dutch auction is strategically equivalent to the first-price sealed-bid auction and the English auction to the second-price sealed-bid auction. Which of these equivalences can fail in a common-value auction with three or more bidders?
options: The English–second-price one: observed drop-out prices reveal rivals' signals while the auction runs, which a sealed bid cannot use.
The Dutch–first-price one: the falling clock reveals that no rival has yet accepted, information a sealed bid cannot use.
Both: in any open format bidders observe rivals' actions before the auction ends and can update their estimate of $v$.
Neither: strategic equivalence rests on the payment rule alone, so what bidders know about $v$ cannot affect it.

questions.question: In a common-value auction the value $v$ is increasing in every bidder's signal (for instance $v=\theta_1+\dots+\theta_n$), signals are continuous, and all bidders use the same strictly increasing bidding function. What does winning tell a bidder about her rivals' signals and about $v$?
options: That the rivals' signals are all below hers, which lowers her expected value of $v$.
Nothing: the signals are independent, so the rivals' signals remain as uncertain as before.
That the rivals' signals are all above hers, which raises her expected value of $v$.
That the rivals' signals equal hers, since the same function maps equal signals to equal bids.
